Listen to this article Share If you lost your job or your primary source of income today, how much of your financial life would remain standing? It is a question every professional, business owner and family should consider. Many people work hard, earn good salaries, receive bonuses or run profitable businesses. Yet, when their primary income stops, their financial progress can quickly begin to unravel. This is because earning money and building wealth are two different things. Income pays for today’s needs. Wealth, when properly structured, can continue supporting you tomorrow. One way to build that structure is to understand four broad asset classes: Business, Commodities, Real Estate and Paper Assets. Each serves a different purpose, carries different risks and can play a role in a broader wealth-building strategy. The goal is not necessarily to own all four immediately, but to understand how they can complement one another. 1. Business: Build or Participate in an Income-Producing Enterprise A business can be a powerful wealth-building asset because it can generate profits, expand operations, employ people and create opportunities for growth. You may build your own business, become a partner in an existing enterprise or invest in another person’s business through equity, subject to the relevant legal and financial arrangements. This matters because wealth-building is not reserved for entrepreneurs. A professional who earns a salary can invest in a viable business without leaving paid employment. The key is to conduct proper due diligence, understand the ownership structure and assess the risks before committing money. Business ownership also carries substantial risks. Businesses can fail, partners can disagree, profits can decline and investments may be difficult to sell. A successful business may also depend heavily on its founder. The lesson is not that everyone should start a business. It is that people can explore ways to participate in productive economic activity beyond earning a salary alone. 2. Commodities: Consider the Things the World Needs Commodities include resources such as gold, silver, crude oil and agricultural products. Their prices are influenced by factors such as supply and demand, global economic conditions, currency movements and geopolitical events. Some investors use certain commodities, particularly gold, as a potential store of value or as a way to diversify a portfolio. Others seek exposure to commodity prices because they believe those prices may rise. But commodities do not all behave alike, and their prices can be volatile. Physical gold, for instance, does not ordinarily generate rental income, dividends or interest. Returns depend largely on price movements, less the costs of acquiring, storing and selling it. Commodities can play a role in a financial plan, but they should not be treated as a guaranteed hedge against every economic problem. The objective is to understand why you are buying a particular asset and what role it is expected to play in your portfolio. 3. Real Estate: Own More Than the Place You Live Real estate is often the first asset class that comes to mind when people think about wealth. In Nigeria, property ownership is frequently associated with financial success. A person who owns land, a residential building or commercial property is often considered to have made it. Property can indeed be a valuable asset. It may generate rental income, appreciate over time and provide a measure of security when properly acquired and managed. However, there is an important distinction between owning a home for personal use and owning property as an investment. Your residence may provide security and reduce your exposure to rising rents, but it may not generate cash for your daily expenses. A rental property, on the other hand, may produce income, although maintenance, vacancies, taxes, legal costs and other expenses can reduce the returns. Property also comes with challenges. It may take time to sell, ownership documents must be verified, and a substantial amount of money can become tied up in one location. Real estate is therefore not simply about buying land. It is about understanding the purpose of the purchase, the costs involved and how the property fits into your wider financial plan. 4. Paper Assets: Let Your Money Participate in Financial Markets Paper assets include financial investments such as stocks, bonds, treasury bills and mutual funds. They offer individuals opportunities to participate in financial markets without having to establish and operate a business or personally manage a physical property. For example, someone earning a salary can invest in shares of a company and potentially benefit from dividends and increases in share prices. Another investor might purchase government securities that pay interest according to their terms. A mutual fund can provide access to a portfolio of investments managed under a defined strategy. These investments serve different purposes. Shares carry market risk, bonds expose investors to risks including interest-rate and credit risk, while treasury bills have their own reinvestment and inflation considerations. Mutual funds vary according to their underlying assets and investment objectives. The advantage is flexibility. Some investments can be purchased in relatively small amounts, and many market-traded instruments are easier to sell than physical property. However, paper assets are not automatically safe simply because they are professionally managed or traded on a recognised market. Investors need to understand what they own, the risks involved, the fees charged and whether the investment aligns with their goals and time horizon. The important lesson is that you do not need to own a company outright to participate in business ownership. Through equity investments, you can own a portion of businesses established and operated by others. Why Relying on One Source Can Be Dangerous Imagine two professionals who each earn ₦1 million monthly. The first spends nearly all the money on living expenses and obligations. The second meets those obligations while gradually building an investment portfolio, perhaps combining suitable financial investments with a carefully researched property or business investment. Their salaries may be identical, but their financial positions can develop very differently over time. The second professional is not necessarily wealthier today. Nor is the strategy guaranteed to succeed. But that person is deliberately building assets that may provide additional income, capital growth or other financial benefits in the future. This is the point of diversification: reducing excessive dependence on one source of income or one category of investment. However, owning four asset classes does not automatically mean you have a diversified portfolio. Four properties in one neighbourhood, for example, may expose you to similar risks. A business, its premises and the family’s entire investment portfolio may also depend on the same local economic conditions. True diversification requires attention to the risks that assets share, not simply the number of assets owned. Where Should You Begin? You do not need to acquire all four asset classes at once. Begin by understanding your income, expenses, debts, emergency reserves, financial responsibilities and goals. Protect yourself against significant financial risks and ensure that you can meet your immediate obligations. Then determine how much you can consistently set aside for investment. Learn about each asset class before committing money. Consider liquidity, expected returns, costs, time horizon and your ability to withstand losses. Diversification should be appropriate to your circumstances, not an excuse to invest in things you do not understand. Your salary or business income may be the engine that starts your wealth-building journey. But over time, your decisions about what to do with that income can determine how much financial resilience you develop. Do not spend your entire working life earning money without deliberately building the assets that could support you when you no longer want, or are no longer able, to work.
